title: TB2-03219
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX(the claimant), and her son, XXXX XXXX XXXX are citizens of the People's Republic of China. The claimant claims to have well-founded fear of persecution at the hands of the Communist regime and in particular, the Public Security Bureau, by reason of her religion as a Christian and her son as a member of a particular social group under sections 96 and 97 of The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1
The claimant was appointed the designated representative of her son, a minor.

The claimant alleges in her Personal Information Form2 that as a result of going through a divorce, she turned to an underground Christian church on the recommendation of a friend. The claimant maintains that she started to attend the underground Christian church in XXXX 2011. The claimant indicated that on XXXX XXXX, 2012, her underground Christian church was raided by the Public Security Bureau (the PSB). The claimant indicated that she was able to escape and went to the home of a relative. The claimant alleges that the PSB went to her home to arrest her for her underground Christian church activities. The claimant stated that arrangements were made with a snakehead (smuggler) to leave the country. The claimant came to Canada on or about February 11, 2012, and claimed for refugee protection a few days later.

I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. I find that the claimants have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that on the balance of probabilities they would personally be subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to the People's Republic of China.

The claimant's oral testimony and the supporting documents filed3 establish their identities as citizens of the People's Republic of China. The claimant as a Member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a member of an underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant indicated that at her underground church in which approximately ten people were present, the members would pray, read the Bible, then discuss it and then members would give testimonials. No further description was provided. When asked by her counsel the biggest difference between practising her religion in the People's Republic of China and Canada, she stated that in Canada, for baptism, there is full immersion in the water but in the People's Republic of China, only sprinkling of water. When asked again about any other differences in the practice of her religion, the claimant stated that in Canada, one can get baptised in the lake. The claimant did not provide any other differences in the practice of her religion in the People's Republic of China and Canada. The claimant failed to indicate that in Canada, she went to a structured building of a church, sang hymns, there was no need for lookouts for the police and that there was a pastor every week at the services. The claimant indicated that the PSB raided her underground church on XXXX XXXX, 2012. The claimant indicated that she ran out of the back door as the PSB were arriving in the front door. The claimant was asked if the PSB were the professional police force for the People's Republic of China, to which she answered in the affirmative. The claimant was asked if the PSB were going to raid her underground church, would they not have surrounded the building and not simply go to the front door so people could run out the back door. The claimant replied that she did not know. I reject this explanation. If the PSB, the professional police force for the People's Republic of China were going to raid this underground church, they would have surrounded the building and not simply go to the front door so people could run out the back door. In summary, I find that the claimant was never a member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China, due to her extremely limited differences in practising her religion in the People's Republic of China and here in Canada as well as the implausible and not credible of the PSB running in the front door so she could run out the back door.

To support her claim, the claimant advised that she is wanted by the PSB, they filed a summons.4 The summons does not indicate that it is an "Arrest Summons" and that it is simply for the claimant to appear. However, the claimant indicated that she would be arrested once she attended at the PSB office. Furthermore, as indicated in the decision of Huang v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), "overall credibility may affect the weight given to the documentary evidence".5 I am mindful of the presence of fraudulent documents6 from the People's Republic of China and since I have found that the claimant was not a member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China I therefore do not find that the summons proffered by the claimant to be authentic. The claimant filed a letter7 from a friend in the People's Republic of China indicating that the underground church was in fact raided. I do not give this document any weight as the author was not present to determine the veracity of it and also I have found that the claimant was not a member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant as a Christian in Canada

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is a Christian in Canada. The claimant was able to answer most questions posed to her on Christianity. Furthermore, the claimant filed Certificates of Baptism for herself and the minor claimant, as well as a church letter dated January 5, 2018, attesting to her membership in that church from February 26, 2012.8 Situation of Christians in Fujian Province

I must determine, whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if she returns to the People's Republic of China and chooses to become a member of an underground Christian church. I am guided by the country conditions documents in evidence.9 According to the United States International Religious Freedom Report for China,10 there are 70 million Christians of which many experts believe are underestimated. According to the most recent outside surveys by Pew in 2010 and 2012, there are 68 million Protestants with 23 million affiliated with state sanctioned umbrella organizations only.11

I note the documentary evidence suggests by virtue of the absence of evidence of incidents of persecution in Fujian has the most liberal policy on religion in the People's Republic of China. The claimant had indicated that the raid took place on XXXX XXXX, 2012, and that two people had been arrested. I have reviewed the entire country document12 package provided by counsel as well as the National Document Packages13 filed by the Board and found only four incidents in Fujian: one, involving a church built in Fuqing that was forcibly demolished. It was not clear whether this church was an underground one or a patriotic church.14 The second incident was in 2006 that there was a demolition of a house church somewhere in Fujian and a demolition of a house church in 2006 in Pingtan County, Fujian and the last in October 2010 that a worker was taken away and sealed three venues used for church gatherings of a church in Lianjiang County in Fujian described as having a strong heart for evangelism.15 There were reports that certain cult type religions, such as the Shouters or Eastern Lightning that the PSB did crack down on those groups, but nothing with respect to Pentecostal (which the claimant has indicated she is) or any other more mainstream Protestant faiths.

The report of Professor T. Lambert indicates that the religious policy in Fujian as relatively liberal and that it has a thriving and rapidly growing Christian community. The report also indicates that 26% of the population are Christian as of 2006.16 Professor Lambert's characterization of Fujian as a relatively liberal province in relation to religious policy was supported by a Canadian government fact-finding mission to the province in 2000 and the executive secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council in 2005. A 2009 report on the Protestant Church in Fujian Province in a Global Chinese Ministries newsletter confirms that there are large numbers of independent house churches in Fujian. The report also indicates that in general, local government in Fujian seems fairly tolerant of unregistered believers as it is rare that one reads of cases of persecution of house church Christians in this province.17 Fujian is rarely mentioned in reports on breaches of religious freedom by the US Department of State, the United States Commission on International Freedom, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch or the various Christian NGOs that report on China. 18

I have considered all of the documents submitted about the situation for Christians in the People's Republic of China, specifically articles and reports documenting arrests and persecution. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that if there were arrests of Christians in Fujian in 2012 or thereafter, there would be some documentation of these arrests.

The principle in Maldonado19 is that when a refugee claimant swears to tell the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there are reasons to doubt their truthfulness.

However, the presumption that a claimant's own testimony is true is always rebuttable and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect to mention.20 There are a number of observers, such as the China Aid Association, the United States Department of State, Asia News, numerous news agencies, Cardinal Kung Foundation, Freedom House21 to name a few. These observers strive to inform the world that religious persecution takes place in the People's Republic of China. In the case of underground Christian house churches, there is information detailing very specific examples of persecution from areas much more remote and difficult to access than Fujian Province. One would expect that an egregious incident such as alleged by the claimant, where two church members were arrested, would be reported.

I am supported in this analysis by the Federal Court decision22 by Justice Crampton who found that it was reasonable for the Board to find that, if underground Christians faced a serious possibility of persecution in Fujian Province, it would have been documented.

As has been discussed, the supporting documentary evidence for the claimant's home province of Fujian indicates, the risk of persecution for practising Christians is low. I recognize that even if the evidence speaks of some harm that would qualify as serious, I must consider whether there is a serious possibility that the harm will actually come to pass. A statute, which outlaws the claimant's conduct or characteristic, may be in existence, and it may provide for unconscionably severe punishment for that conduct or characteristic, but this does not necessarily mean there is a serious possibility that the punishment will be inflicted on the claimant. The Supreme Court has emphasized that, in a determination as to whether the claimant's fear is objectively well founded, the relevant factors include the laws in the claimant's homeland, together with the manner in which they are applied. In this connection, the Court cited paragraph 43 of the UNHCR Handbook.23

This leads me to determine that the claimant (and the minor claimant) are free to choose to worship in the Christian congregation of her choosing. I have chosen to rely on the documentary evidence because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources, which would reasonably be expected to be knowledgeable with respect to the situation of Christians in Fujian. The documentary evidence is seen as reliable, probative, detailed information, so as to provide me with a thorough understanding of the situation of the Christian church in Fujian Province.

I have considered the documentary evidence and I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant (and the minor claimant) would be able to practice their religion in any church in Fujian Province if they were to return to the their home in Fujian province in the People's Republic of China and that there is not a serious possibility that they would be persecuted for doing so.

I am supported in this decision by a decision of Mr. Justice Russell.24 In reaching his decision, Mr. Justice Russell cited Justice Crampton's decision in Nen Mei Lin25concerning Fujian Province in which the court stated that in the context of the significant detail in the documentation regarding the dates and locations of arrests and other steps taken to discourage Christian activity in the People's Republic of China, it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian Province it would have been documented. In addition, Justice Lemieux in Jiang26 noted that the documentary evidence concerning Fujian Province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice and people generally practice their religion freely.

In another Federal Court decision in the case of Yao27 Justice O'Keefe notes that "this Court has held on several occasions that the Board's finding that Christians may practice freely in Fujian Province is reasonable". Concerns of Forcible IUD for Family Planning

The claimant, when asked by the panel, as to what she fears if she were to return to the People's Republic of China, indicated that she would be arrested by the PSB for activities at her underground church. It was not until her counsel prompted her as to what else she fears if she returns to her home country that she mentioned that she does not want to be forced to wear an IUD, as she now has two children: one born in the People's Republic of China and one born in Canada. When asked by the panel why she did not indicate her fear of being forced to wear an IUD, the claimant replied that she was too nervous. I reject this explanation, as the fear of forced type of birth control is a major part of her claim.

The claimant has two children as previously indicated, one born in Canada and one born in the People's Republic of China. I find that the child born in Canada would not be considered in determining the number of children for family planning purposes in the People's Republic of China. Article 10 of the Regulations of Fujian Province on Population and Family Planning28states: When both the husband and wife are Chinese returned from overseas, whose children were born overseas and are residents of foreign countries before they returned to China for settlement, the number of such children of theirs shall not be counted towards the number of children in this Regulation on Population and Family Planning.

Although the claimant is single and her Canadian-born child born out of wedlock, country documentation29 indicates that children who are born out of wedlock should not be discriminated against and shall enjoy the same rights as children born in wedlock. Therefore, I find that the claimant would not be forced to wear an IUD upon returning to the People's Republic of China as her Canadian-born child would not be counted towards the two-child family planning policy in the People's Republic of China.

In the alternative, if the Canadian-born child of the claimant is counted towards the two-child family planning in the People's Republic of China, she would not be forced to wear an IUD, as Article 16 of the Regulations of Fujian Province on Population and Family Planning30 states that in order to practice family planning, couples who already have children may choose to adopt safe, effective and appropriate contraceptive and birth control measures to prevent and reduce the incidence of unwanted pregnancies. I find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant could choose her own method of birth control. Furthermore, the claimant maintains that she does not have her family planning/IUD booklet since it was taken by family planning officials and thus, she may not have to report to them at all.
Based on the totality of the evidence in this particular case, I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees under s. 96 nor persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the Act.

The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims. (signed) "Diane L. Tinker" Diane L.
